Bendale-Glen Andrew: Developed in the 1950s–60s as part of Scarborough's postwar residential expansion, Bendale is a quiet mid-century suburb anchored by a ravine system and a strong South Asian community — particularly Punjabi and Tamil families who have made these English-named streets their own. The contrast between the neighbourhood's Tudor place names and its present-day households tells the layered settlement story that defines Scarborough. The Bendale ravine edges offer unexpected pockets of urban wilderness just minutes from the main commercial strip on Lawrence.
East L'Amoreaux: Named after the L'Amoreaux family — among Scarborough's earliest European settlers, who farmed this land in the early 1800s — this neighbourhood has been thoroughly remade by postwar immigration. Today it has a strong Chinese and South Asian character, anchored by the Bridlewood Community Centre and the commercial strips of Sheppard and Warden. The tension between its pastoral settler name and its diasporic present is exactly the kind of story Scarborough tells with particular power.
L'Amoreaux West: The western flank of the L'Amoreaux community shares its 19th-century settler name with its eastern neighbour but developed its own suburban character through the 1970s–80s. L'Amoreaux Park — one of Scarborough's largest greenspaces — anchors the neighbourhood with sports fields, a pond, and a community centre frequented by families from across the surrounding newcomer communities. The park's quiet weekday mornings and crowded weekend afternoons are two entirely different documentary worlds.
Malvern East: Malvern is one of Scarborough's most historically significant communities — a planned suburban development from the 1970s that became home to successive waves of Caribbean, South Asian, and East African newcomers. Malvern East is the quieter residential flank, with mid-rise townhouses and community parks that become outdoor living rooms in summer. Its story is one of postwar suburban planning meeting the realities of working-class immigrant settlement.
Malvern West: The western half of Malvern carries the neighbourhood's commercial energy, including Malvern Town Centre and a hub of community services. Originally designed for white middle-class families, Malvern today is one of Toronto's most proudly diverse communities — with strong Caribbean, Somali, and Tamil presences — and its designation as a city 'priority neighbourhood' through the 2000s shaped both its struggles and its remarkable tradition of community organizing.
Morningside Heights: A 1980s–90s subdivision in north Scarborough, developed at the edge of the Highland Creek watershed, Morningside Heights sits at one of the higher elevations in the borough. Its relatively recent residential streets have a clean suburban geometry that attracted South Asian and Chinese families seeking good schools and green surroundings. The ravine edges on its eastern and southern flanks offer sudden, disorienting contact with deep urban forest just steps from the sidewalk.
West Rouge: Scarborough's far eastern edge meets the Rouge River watershed here — one of the largest urban river systems in North America. The Rouge National Urban Park stretches north from West Rouge's edge, a remarkable piece of wilderness preserved within the city limits. The Rouge Beach and river mouth are among the most scenically distinctive locations in all of Toronto: a place where the city and the wild hold an uneasy, beautiful truce.
Woburn North: The northern extension of the historic Woburn community, which takes its name from the English county town near London. Postwar bungalows along wide suburban streets were built in the 1960s–70s for working-class families, many of them British. Today the same streets shelter South Asian and Caribbean households — the English place name now a quiet piece of irony overlaid on a community that has nothing to do with England.
Golfdale-Cedarbrae-Woburn: This stretch of central Scarborough has evolved into one of the richest corridors of Afro-Caribbean and South Asian commercial life in the city. Lawrence Avenue East here is thick with Jamaican bakeries, South Asian grocers, and hair braiding salons that tell the story of how Black and brown communities migrated outward from downtown Toronto through the 1980s and 90s. The neighbourhood's everyday commercial strip is documentary material of the first order.
Guildwood: Home to the Guild Park Estate — one of the most cinematically haunting locations in Toronto — a lakefront property that once housed the Guild of All Arts creative colony and now displays rescued architectural fragments from demolished Toronto buildings. The neighbourhood itself is a leafy postwar enclave on the Bluffs edge with winding streets and deep ravines. For a documentary, Guildwood offers the surreal beauty of Greek columns standing in a suburban garden, and the quiet of mid-century homes that have watched the city change around them.
Scarborough Village: One of the oldest named communities in the area, Scarborough Village sits above the Bluffs along Kingston Road — the historic east-west route from downtown Toronto. Its modest, working-class character and tight-knit community have resisted the gentrification pressure that has begun remaking the western end of the Bluffs. Proximity to Scarborough Bluffs Park gives it dramatic natural scenery just minutes from everyday bungalow life.
Eglinton East: The stretch of Eglinton Avenue through this neighbourhood is one of Scarborough's defining commercial corridors — dense with South Asian businesses, storefront churches, and community services. This is working Scarborough: economically mixed, densely settled, with a streetscape shaped by decades of immigrant entrepreneurship. The Eglinton Crosstown LRT now under construction will finally connect this corridor to the transit grid, remaking both its accessibility and its property market.
West Hill: A postwar neighbourhood at Scarborough's eastern edge, bounded by Highland Creek to the east and Kingston Road to the south, West Hill has a strong Caribbean-Canadian community anchored by its churches. Colonel Danforth Park follows the Highland Creek ravine through the neighbourhood — a green corridor that has quietly sustained community life for decades. West Hill is the kind of neighbourhood that gets left out of Toronto's cultural narrative but carries stories worth telling.
Morningside: Morningside sits at the junction of two Scarboroughs — the postwar suburban fabric to the north and the older, denser communities near Eglinton to the south. Morningside Park runs through it, providing a green backbone for immigrant communities that are primarily South Asian and East African. Morningside Avenue on a summer afternoon is a compact documentary portrait of contemporary Scarborough.
Highland Creek: The historic village of Highland Creek is one of the oldest continuously settled places in Scarborough, with roots going back to the 1790s when Empire Loyalists moved north from the new United States. The University of Toronto Scarborough campus anchors the neighbourhood today, drawing a young, diverse academic community. The Highland Creek valley itself is one of the most beautiful ravine landscapes in the city — mature forest, meadows, and a creek that has carved through the shale over millennia.
Centennial Scarborough: Named for Canada's centennial year of 1967, when this neighbourhood was developed as suburban housing for the postwar boom, Centennial today sits within the orbit of UTSC and has a strong student and newcomer character. Its mid-century architectural details survive in bungalows now home to families whose connection to the neighbourhood's centennial origins is purely geographic. The name itself is a time stamp on the city's confident postwar expansion.
Milliken: Straddling the Toronto–Markham boundary, Milliken is anchored by Pacific Mall — one of the largest Chinese indoor shopping malls in North America. The neighbourhood has one of the highest concentrations of Chinese-Canadians in Toronto, and its streetscape of bubble tea shops, dim sum restaurants, and Chinese-language schools is a vivid portrait of diasporic culture in suburban form. Milliken tells the story of how immigration can comprehensively remake suburban geography.
Agincourt North: Named after the famous 1415 battle in northern France, Agincourt is one of Scarborough's most historically layered suburb names. The northern part of the neighbourhood developed in the 1960s–70s, originally attracting working-class British and Italian families. Today it has a significant Chinese population anchoring the Agincourt retail corridor, while golf courses and parks along the northern fringe give it an unexpectedly spacious, green quality.
Agincourt South-Malvern West: The southern half of Agincourt merges into Malvern's western edge, creating one of the most densely diverse corridors in Scarborough. Kennedy Road and Sheppard Avenue East form its main axes — commercially vibrant, ethnically layered, perpetually in motion. This neighbourhood has undergone extraordinary demographic change over four decades: from postwar British-immigrant suburb to one of the most ethnically mixed census tracts in Canada.
Dorset Park: Dorset Park sits at the densely populated convergence of Kennedy Road and Lawrence Avenue East, with a high concentration of social housing, community services, and a community that has absorbed generations of newcomers under difficult economic conditions. Organizations like the Dorset Park Health Hub have built a remarkable local infrastructure in response. This is documentary territory — complicated, real, and underrepresented in Toronto's stories about itself.
Ionview: A compact postwar community between Birchmount Road and Kennedy Road, Ionview's name evokes mid-century optimism — the atomic age's vocabulary applied to a quiet residential suburb. Today it is home to a mix of South Asian and Caribbean families whose daily lives unfold along modest streets backing onto the Taylor-Massey Creek ravine. The neighbourhood is a small, intact piece of postwar suburban Toronto that has absorbed a new community without erasing its original form.
Kennedy Park: Named for the major road that defines its western edge, Kennedy Park grew through the 1950s–60s as a working-class postwar neighbourhood of bungalows and small lots. Today it is one of the more economically pressured parts of Scarborough, with significant Toronto Community Housing and community organizations working to address longstanding inequalities. Kennedy Park is underrepresented in Toronto's cultural narrative and exactly the kind of place a documentary about Scarborough should not skip.
Cliffcrest: Perched on the Scarborough Bluffs above Lake Ontario, Cliffcrest has one of the most dramatic natural settings of any Toronto neighbourhood. Cathedral Bluffs Park — with its towering clay cliffs plunging to the lake — is the defining feature, and the neighbourhood's mid-century bungalows sit on streets with unexpected ravine-edge lots and lake views. The tension between ordinary suburban domesticity and extraordinary geological drama makes Cliffcrest unforgettable on screen.
Birchcliffe-Cliffside: The southwestern corner of Scarborough, abutting the older city proper, Birchcliffe-Cliffside has a tighter, more urban fabric than most of the borough. Kingston Road here is lined with independent shops, galleries, and cafes — a stretch that feels like what other Scarborough commercial strips might become. The Bluffs are accessible at several points, and the neighbourhood marks the geographic threshold where Toronto's older urban form transitions into Scarborough's more open suburban landscape.
Bendale South: The southern portion of Bendale stretches toward Lawrence Avenue East, quiet and residential with a strong South Asian presence — particularly Punjabi and Tamil families who have made these mid-century streets their own. Proximity to Scarborough Town Centre has brought increasing condo development to the edges, layering newer density over older bungalow streets. Bendale South is a neighbourhood in the middle of a quiet, incremental transformation.
Oakridge: One of Scarborough's smaller residential pockets, Oakridge sits between Victoria Park and Warden, south of Eglinton — close enough to the old city border to have a slightly denser, older street form. A diverse Caribbean and South Asian population has reshaped the neighbourhood from its postwar origins. Small parks, community housing, and modest 1960s-era homes give it a lived-in, unassuming quality that rewards patient attention.
Clairlea-Birchmount: The westernmost sliver of Scarborough, Clairlea-Birchmount sits along the old Danforth and O'Connor corridors where Scarborough and East York historically blurred together. The Taylor-Massey Creek runs through it, a green corridor connecting this corner of the city eastward through the larger Scarborough ravine network. Early 20th-century homes and postwar bungalows sit in close proximity to one of the most underappreciated ravine systems in Toronto.
Wexford/Maryvale: Wexford developed in the 1920s–50s with a pronounced Irish-Catholic character — its name comes from County Wexford — and still carries traces of that origin in its institutional architecture. Today it is home to a large Filipino-Canadian and Italian-Canadian community, and the Wexford Collegiate School for the Arts has made it a producing ground for Canadian musicians, actors, and dancers. There is a particular creative energy in Wexford that the rest of Scarborough doesn't quite replicate.
Tam O'Shanter-Sullivan: Named after the Tam O'Shanter Golf Course that once dominated the neighbourhood's northern edge, this northeast Scarborough community has a quiet residential character that belies its proximity to major commercial arterials. The golf course land was a defining feature of the neighbourhood's identity for decades; its eventual redevelopment tells a story of how urban green space gets — or doesn't get — prioritized in the suburban city. Today the area has a significant Chinese and South Asian population living in a landscape still shaped by the golf-era layout.
Steeles: The northernmost strip of Scarborough runs along Steeles Avenue at the city boundary with Markham, and it feels like a threshold — neither fully city nor fully suburb. The Steeles commercial corridor mixes warehouses, strip malls, and restaurants, transitioning gradually into the Pacific Mall cultural geography of Milliken. Steeles is Scarborough at its most liminal, and liminality is always interesting to document.
